title: Create Compelling Spectacles
summary: Words invite dispute; images bypass it. Stage the arresting picture and the argument dissolves before it begins.
core: Most people trust their eyes more than their ears. Language is easily misquoted, mistranslated and turned back on the speaker, whereas an image, a colour or a ritual arrives already interpreted and meets emotion directly rather than reason. Visible form is therefore the superior instrument of influence, since whoever controls how he is seen controls the terms on which he is judged. A spectacle does not only impress an audience; it occupies it, suspending the descent into scepticism. The wise operator does not explain himself, because explanation places him on the defensive and hands the argument to others. He builds an image vivid enough that the audience does the believing for him.
observance: Diane de Poitiers held Henry II of France for three decades through imagery rather than argument. She made the hunting goddess Diana her emblem, had the sculptor Jean Goujon carve the fountain and reclining figure at her chateau of Anet, and took the goddess's attributes, the crescent, the bow, the hounds and the stag. She wore black and white, the colours of mourning and of the moon. Her letters to the king were signed jointly with his, their initials interlaced as one monogram, and that monogram appeared on the columns, doorways, ceilings and plate of Anet and in the stone of Chenonceau, which Catherine de Medici tried in vain to erase. He read the goddess as a claim that his love was sacred, and gave her a duchy and a fortune.
transgression: Thomas Paine built the most powerful political force in the English-speaking world out of words alone. Common Sense, The American Crisis and Rights of Man moved continents, yet Paine possessed no image, no institution, no uniform, no court and no patron. The American revolution did not enshrine him, and France summoned him to Paris in 1792 only to find him without a following and to jail him when the Terror began. He returned home and spent his last years in a borrowed cottage in New Rochelle, largely friendless, and died in 1809 while his own country looked elsewhere. Persuasion can seize power and surrender it within a generation, because a man who offers only arguments asks his audience to supply the emotion themselves.
reversal: A spectacle conceals as much as it proclaims, and concealment is not free. Design that flatters its maker becomes a public claim, and the crowd will eventually audit it. If the imagery outruns the substance, the gap reads as a lie to the very audience it dazzled, and a leader who has spent his credit on a stage has little left when the programme fails. Scale is costly too, since each colossus makes the next one smaller. A prudent operator keeps one anchor of plainness, a familiar face and an unremarkable habit, so that the spectacle reads as character rather than as ambition.
keyTakeaways: Images arrive already interpreted; words can be quoted and turned back on you.
Stage the arresting picture rather than explaining yourself and becoming defensive.
If the imagery outruns the substance, the audience reads the gap as a lie.
Keep one anchor of plainness, so the spectacle reads as character and not ambition.

title: Think as you like but Behave like others
summary: Keep your convictions in reserve and wear the manners of the room. Visible difference invites quiet punishment.
core: Private belief is cheap and public conformity is expensive, and the law insists on paying the cheap price. Most people hold their convictions as inherited furniture rather than examined conclusions, so an argument aimed at them reads as an insult rather than a correction. Unconventional conduct is worse, since it signals contempt: a man who dresses strangely or professes contempt for the crowd declares their lives lesser than his own. People punish that insult quietly, through neglect, rumour and delay. The counsel is therefore to blend, cultivate the common touch, and reserve originality for the inner circle. Conformity buys what power cannot do without, which is the room in which an unorthodox idea can be planted.
observance: Franklin D. Roosevelt governed through the most ordinary man available. He dressed plainly, was photographed with a cigarette and a cane, named a political adversary a friend, and made the press conference and the fireside chat into the office's proper instrument rather than the oratory it was supposed to require. He dramatised himself as an ordinary citizen with a disability, referred to the people as his friends, and placed himself inside the domestic sitting rooms of America rather than above them. Theodore Roosevelt had warned that a president should be treated as a bullfrog sharing the pool; the same instinct, better executed, carried the youngest man ever elected president through four elections and two terms.
transgression: Pausanias, the Spartan regent who commanded the allied Greeks at Plataea in 479 BC, lost the leadership of the Hellenic League by adopting Persian dress and manners. He travelled with a guard of Medes and Egyptians, dined in the Persian fashion, made himself difficult to approach, and placed an inscription at Delphi claiming the victory over the Persians as his own. The recently liberated Ionians found the behaviour intolerable and offered the leadership to Athens. Sparta recalled him and tried him on the gravest charges, acquitting him only for want of evidence. He fled, resumed his treachery, and was finally starved to death in a temple at Taenarus, his aged mother said to have laid the first stone of the masonry that roofed him in.
reversal: The mask is a prison, and the wearer pays most of the bill. A man who spends a lifetime performing the common touch loses the sense of which self is his, and reaches the summit unable to say what he actually wants. If the display is too consistent, with no visible strain, the court concludes the man is performing, and performed humility has always signalled ambition. The exception worth naming is the man who already stands out, where difference registers as distance rather than insult. Even then it is dangerous, because a public accustomed to your strangeness will deny you the ordinary approval on which any position secretly depends.
keyTakeaways: Keep convictions private and wear the room's manners; visible difference reads as contempt.
Blend into the crowd, because unorthodox conduct invites quiet punishment.
Conformity buys you the room in which an unorthodox idea can be planted.
A lifetime of performing the common touch leaves you unsure which self is yours.

title: Stir up Waters to Catch Fish
summary: Still water gives your opponent room to plot. Provoke the other to lose his temper while you keep yours.
core: Emotion is a strategist's error. An angry man acts before he is ready, misjudges his opponent and overreaches on the belief that force of feeling has become force of will. The man who stays composed while his adversary is agitated controls the tempo of the encounter, because the angrier man is always deciding at the wrong moment. The law adds the aggressive corollary. It is not enough to be calm; it is worth deliberately provoking, since a challenger goaded into revealing his plan has given a gift, and one goaded into boasting has disarmed himself in public. Anger is not a vice to be cured but an instrument to be withheld from others and rationed for oneself.
observance: Haile Selassie handled the treachery of his son-in-law, Haile Selassie Gugsa, with a patience that never required a raised voice. Gugsa had gone over to the Italians, been given the title of Ras and ruled Tigray as a puppet governor, and his defection had already cost the emperor that province. Selassie let him remain in place, allowed the treason to mature, and waited while a man whose vanity had put him there convinced himself he had been restored. When Gugsa finally marched on Addis Ababa, the emperor had already turned his officers, isolated the rebel and met him with loyal troops. Gugsa was extradited after years of British custody, tried in 1947 and imprisoned for the rest of his life. The stable calm was the weapon; the execution of the verdict was administrative.
transgression: Napoleon Bonaparte lost control of his ministers in the council of January 1809. Talleyrand, the foreign minister, and Joseph Fouche, the minister of police, had been quietly corresponding about the succession should the emperor fall in Spain, and interception of their letters removed all doubt. Napoleon, back in Paris sooner than announced, delivered a sustained attack on Talleyrand for the better part of half an hour, ending in an insult about a silk stocking. Talleyrand stood through it and left remarking to the council that it was a pity so great a man had so bad a manner. Napoleon stripped him of office the next day. Fouche, the more dangerous of the two, was untouched because the Emperor could not spare him. The outburst settled nothing and showed every minister how a crisis would be handled.
reversal: There are fish that should not be roused. To taunt an opponent whose resources exceed your own, or whose temperament you have misread, is to invite a blow you cannot survive, and a patient rival will simply let you exhaust yourself in the water you have stirred. The technique also decays with use. A thunderbolt delivered once is frightening; delivered monthly it becomes theatre, and those who witness it learn to discount it. Manufactured anger in particular appears on cue and vanishes at the same word, and is seen through instantly. If you find yourself inventing rage to discipline a room, the room has understood that the fear was manufactured, and what remains is a man who needs to be feared and no longer is.
keyTakeaways: Stay composed while the other side is forced to decide at the wrong moment.
Provoke a rival into revealing a plan or boasting; anger is their error, not yours.
Let the treachery mature instead of answering it on the day you discover it.
Manufactured rage appears on cue, and the room quickly learns to discount it.

title: Despise the Free Lunch
summary: What arrives without a price is not a gift but an invoice, itemised later. Pay full value and keep your name off the ledger.
core: Anything offered for nothing is either a trick or a debt, and both bind the receiver more tightly than cash. A gift accepted without examination creates gratitude, and gratitude is a leash: the recipient becomes hard to dismiss and easy to move. Paying full price leaves the transaction clean, with no one to whom you are obliged and nothing held as favour. The law extends the principle outward, since money kept idle is money wasted, and generosity circulated buys reputation, loyalty and the gratitude of others. Independence is a form of power, and every free lunch is a mortgage taken against it at a rate the borrower never sees until the terms are read aloud.
observance: Cosimo de' Medici was the wealthiest banker in Europe and behaved throughout his life as though he were not. He ate and drank simply, worked long regular hours, dressed in sober cloth without ostentation, and left himself accessible to the humblest citizens of Florence. He lent to princes, popes and merchant houses and took his profit in interest, a debt that can be measured and repaid, rather than in gratitude, which cannot. When his rivals had him arrested and exiled in 1433 he returned to Florence within a year to a procession of gratitude, which he converted into constitutional influence. His money was spent on churches, art and the purchase of allies. Pope Pius II observed that peace and war were settled in Cosimo's house, and that he chose who filled the public offices.
transgression: The Spanish Empire received the ransom of Atahualpa, the greatest cache of precious metal ever taken in the Americas, and treated it as windfall rather than as a debt. Francisco Pizarro filled a room with gold and twice again with silver, took the crown's fifth, divided the rest among 168 men, and executed the Inca who had kept his side of the bargain. The treasure was spent quickly, much of it by Charles V on German debts and on the defence of Vienna. Men and ships departed for the legendary city of El Dorado, and the crown funded expedition after expedition, draining Seville in pursuit of a fortune that was never found. The bullion hired mercenaries and creditors instead of creating power, and the search for more bullion consumed the attention, the credit and eventually the empire.
reversal: Scepticism has its own failure mode. A man who reads every offer as a trap will refuse help at the moment he most needs it and end his days wealthy, independent and unconnected, which is a poor substitute for standing. Some people give without calculation, and treating all kindness as an invoice wounds the giver and shrinks the giver's own circle. The more serious error runs the other way, since generosity deployed as a technique is easily detected, and recipients who feel purchased become the more dangerous. A useful discipline is to price everything, including your own time, and to keep the ledger visible; then gratitude is a pleasure rather than a claim, and the independence the law defends survives the transaction.
keyTakeaways: Anything offered for nothing is either a trick or a debt, and both of them bind you.
Pay full price, so no one is owed anything and nothing is held as a favour.
Idle money is wasted money; circulate it for standing rather than for gratitude.
Price everything, including your own time, and keep the ledger visible.

title: Avoid Stepping into a Great Man's Shoes
summary: Successors inherit an unfavourable comparison. Change the ground of the contest rather than outdo a legend.
core: Whoever comes second is judged against whoever came first, and the first mover keeps the advantage permanently, because the memory of an original is more vivid than the record of an emulator. A successor who tries to do what the predecessor did better will be found wanting. The law therefore advises a break rather than an improvement: distance yourself from the legend, contrast yourself with it, and hunt for the vacuum, the field nobody has claimed. Symbolism matters, and not trivially, because it tells an audience in an instant which of two possible stories it is living. Inheritance is a ceiling rather than a foundation, and the only genuine inheritance is the name, not the method.
observance: Alexander the Great came to the throne of Macedon as the son of Philip II, the most successful ruler in Greece, and treated the resemblance as a problem rather than a guarantee. Philip was the cautious builder who had kept the treasury full and the army intact; Alexander adopted the opposite profile, aggressive, fast and conspicuously unwilling to be his father's heir. Marching into Asia he came upon the Gordian knot at Gordium, tied by legend to the promise that the man who loosed it would rule Asia. Alexander took his sword and cut it. The gesture told every observer what it was meant to tell them, that the new king would not be bound by precedent or prophecy or by the considered pace of his father.
transgression: Louis XV succeeded his great-grandfather Louis XIV in 1715 at the age of five, and his reign of nearly sixty years was measured against the Sun King's seventy-two from the first day. He did not rebel against the comparison; he entered it. He moved the court back to Versailles, reoccupied the theatre of his great-grandfather's glory, and spent a generation failing inside it. France lost Canada and most of its Indian possessions in the Seven Years' War, the parlements revolted against his ministers, and he was known as the beloved king whose credit had been spent by other men. He handed Louis XVI in 1774 a monarchy weakened, indebted and delegitimised. Fifty years of visible failure to reach a dead man's standard is what happens when the successor accepts the ground of the comparison.
reversal: The break has a cost often understated. A successor who cannot inherit the predecessor's method will hear that he repudiates the thing that made the institution respectable, and the faction loyal to the old way will treat him as a usurper from the first day. Some forms of authority cannot be reinvented, only carried: legal continuity, accumulated trust, the dignity of an office, the habits of an organisation are not spectacles but gravity to be borrowed. And the vacuum is a fantasy more often than a territory; unclaimed ground must still be defended, and the founder who strides into empty space frequently arrives alone. Do not imitate, but inherit deliberately, know which parts of the precedent are load-bearing, and change course only where the old course has demonstrably ended.
keyTakeaways: A successor who competes on the predecessor's ground will be found wanting.
Change the terms of the contest rather than trying to outdo a legend.
Symbolism tells an audience in a moment which of two stories it is living.
Some forms of authority can only be carried; know which parts of precedent are load-bearing.

title: Strike the Shepherd and the Sheep will Scatter
summary: Group disorder usually has an author. Neutralise the one mind giving it shape and the crowd loses its direction.
core: Friction in a body is rarely spontaneous. It is organised, voiced and sustained by somebody who profits from it, and that person, not the crowd, is the problem to be solved. Remove the instigator, isolate him or discredit him openly, and the discontent that looked like a mass movement evaporates, because the followers had been carrying someone else's argument and have none of their own. Negotiation is the temptation and the trap, since the dissenter has no genuine grievance, only a use for grievance, and talking concedes that he is a party to be answered. The judgement is unsentimental. Much of what appears to be a crowd's opinion is one man's opinion with a following, and the sooner that is seen the cheaper the correction.
observance: Athens built an institution to do exactly this. Each year the assembly decided whether to hold an ostracism, and if the question carried, citizens scratched the name of the man they most wanted removed onto a potsherd. If the tally reached six thousand, the man with most votes left the city for ten years with his property and honours intact. The penalty was deliberately mild, the term reversible, the intent preventive rather than punitive. Themistocles was ostracised in 472 or 471 BC at the height of his influence, having lost the confidence of the elite and built a sanctuary whose name advertised his role in saving Greece. Aristides the Just was sent away earlier because his integrity had become a measure of the rest. Both men returned.
transgression: Charles I of England had an opposition with a single identifiable centre in the Earl of Strafford, his most able adviser, and he never struck him. Parliament impeached Strafford in November 1640 and moved toward an attainder; the king's attempt to rescue his minister by seizing the Tower in May 1641 destroyed Strafford instead and cost him the confidence of the peers he was counting on. Strafford was beheaded on Tower Hill before a crowd of perhaps thirty thousand. Then in January 1642 Charles tried the same method against the parliamentary leadership, entering the House of Commons himself with armed men to arrest five members. They were not there. He lost London, was presented to the country as a man who came with soldiers to the parliament, and was executed eight years later.
reversal: Two errors wait on either side. Strike the wrong person and you manufacture the martyr the crowd was waiting for, converting a nuisance into a symbol that unites far more than he ever divided. Wait too long and the flock hardens around its shepherd until removal is impossible. Nor is exile always available, since the platform that spreads a name also magnifies it. Diagnosis is the whole difficulty, because the loudest dissenter is often a symptom of a grievance genuinely held by many. The sound procedure is to remove the instigator without letting the removal read as persecution, to give the underlying grievance something truthful to be answered by, and to act before separate things have fused into one.
keyTakeaways: Most group disorder is organised and voiced by somebody who profits from it.
Remove the instigator and the followers find they have no argument of their own.
Do not negotiate with a dissenter who has only a use for grievance.
Make the removal read as order rather than persecution, or you build a martyr.

title: Work on the Hearts and Minds of Others
summary: Force produces resistance. Convert the person instead, and you buy a loyal ally rather than a defeated subject.
core: Coercion buys compliance and rents it dearly, because it manufactures the resentment that becomes the next crisis. Seduction buys the same result and leaves the convert willing, which is why the law prefers it. The work is patient and requires attention to the individual rather than to the crowd: people move on their own fears, vanities and loves, and a man who has not troubled to learn them has not met them at all. Self-interest is the surest ground, since a noble cause secures only as long as the enthusiasm lasts, while a visible interest secures the act itself. Attention is a form of power and inattention its opposite. An operator who never asks what others want has not met them, and has lost before any negotiation begins.
observance: Zhuge Liang, chancellor of the state of Shu, was given the pacification of the southern districts in 225 and won it without completing a conquest. He learned that the chieftain Meng Huo was respected and followed by the people he governed, and that killing him would only produce another leader in his place. Zhuge Liang captured him, walked him through the Shu camp, and released him; Meng Huo returned, was captured again and released again, through seven captures, each followed by courtesy rather than a sentence. His officers complained that the most important prisoner of the south was being handed back over and over. On the seventh occasion Meng Huo surrendered of his own accord and brought the tribes with him. Nanzhong then supplied the western campaigns with recruits, horses and minerals for a generation.
transgression: Marie Antoinette was described by those who dealt with her as a woman who believed affection and admiration were owed to her because of her position, and that the display was itself the payment. She did not travel among the French, did not receive petitioners, and made no appearance in Paris or the provinces; the court at Versailles, which she enlarged lavishly, became the object of the resentment the monarchy could least afford. The financial crisis of the 1770s supplied the material, and when it came to bread there was no established channel of feeling between the queen and the people who had to eat it. The October Days of 1789 began as a march on Versailles and were never a problem again. She was separated from her child and executed by guillotine in October 1793, without any prior conversation to soften it.
reversal: A seduction that works on an individual does not necessarily scale, and a leader who has learned to move people by their vanities can be moved himself by somebody who has studied his. The method also leaves the operator dependent on continual perception, since maintaining a persona costs attention that would otherwise go to the work. The deepest danger is that attraction and consent are not the same thing, and the law offers no mechanism for telling them apart. Its counsel can be read as a technique for manufacturing agreement without agreement, which is not persuasion but its counterfeit. If the seduced cannot later say yes to what they were moved toward, the alliance was never theirs and will hold exactly as long as the manipulation does.
keyTakeaways: Force buys compliance and rents it dearly, because it manufactures the next crisis.
Learn what each person fears, wants and loves before you make any proposal.
Return a defeated leader to his community; killing him only produces a successor.
Attention is a form of power, and inattention means you have not met them at all.

title: Disarm and Infuriate with the Mirror Effect
summary: Repeat the other's words, methods and values back at them, and you decide whether they are seen or dazzled.
core: Everyone is a little in love with their own reflection, and a man who reflects an opponent's words, methods or deepest convictions back to him becomes suddenly difficult to read. Used on an adversary the mirror is provocative, because a man confronted with his own conduct repeated at him experiences it as mockery and loses balance. Used on a prospective ally or a lover it is disarming, because the rare experience of being exactly understood is almost impossible to refuse. Argument here is the weakest instrument, since the truth is seldom heard and is more often resented than accepted; demonstration persuades. Reflection transfers the initiative, because the opponent must now answer himself, and a man answering himself rarely reaches a favourable conclusion.
observance: Joseph Fouche, minister of police under Napoleon, survived the Consulate, the Empire and the Bourbon Restoration by a method his enemies called an absence of principle. He built a police network that watched his ministers as well as his citizens, kept the Emperor's own dossier among his files, and never allowed himself to be permanently out of favour. When Napoleon's fortunes collapsed, Fouche was again indispensable to Louis XVIII and again quietly marked for removal, and he moved again. He took the governorship of Rome after the expedition to Elba, was suspected in the Malet conspiracy of 1812 and returned a document set to the Emperor that had been declared destroyed. He reflected whichever regime stood in front of him, so each government found a man who had always been one of its own.
transgression: Alcibiades was the most complete mirror in Greek history, and he died because of it. Plutarch described him as capable of transforming himself into the habits of any company better than the chameleon changes colour, and Athens saw it first: he trailed a purple robe through the agora, cut the planks of his own ship so that he could sleep more comfortably, and carried a shield with no ancestral device on it. In Sparta he lived on black broth, took cold baths and let his hair grow, and the Spartans were astonished that a man with a cook and a perfumer had ever existed. In Persia he outdid the satrap Tissaphernes in magnificence. Each group believed it had found a man of its own, and each eventually discovered it had been looking at a reflection of itself. Thebes killed him in Phrygia in 404 BC at the instigation of Sparta.
reversal: The mirror fails in the place it is most used, which is on the people you intend to keep. Repeated reflection of a spouse, an ally or a subordinate is eventually experienced as mockery, and the discovery that you have been studying them produces a betrayal worse than neglect, because it shows the relationship was never what it appeared. Mirroring also produces an invisibility of its own, since a man with no visible position has none to appeal to. The honest technique is to reflect rarely and accurately, to create a moment of genuine understanding rather than a habit, and to be visibly yourself with those whose regard matters.
keyTakeaways: Repeat their words, methods and values back until they must answer themselves.
Argument is the weakest instrument here, since the truth is resented more often than heard.
Being exactly understood is nearly impossible for a prospective ally to refuse.
Mirror enemies occasionally; mirroring the people you want to keep reads as mockery.

title: Preach the Need for Change, but Never Reform too much at once
summary: Everyone endorses change in the abstract and resists it on Tuesday. Dress the reform as an improvement on what exists.
core: The abstract case for reform is agreed to by nearly everyone who is not currently being reformed. Resistance lies in habit, in status, and in the difficulty of imagining life after a change one has not chosen. Applied hard, reform is experienced as loss, and a population told for years that it is being improved will resist the improvement on principle. The remedy is not less ambition but better timing. Announce the necessity of change, keep the forms people recognise, retain the ceremonies and titles and institutional shapes, and change what lies behind them, so that the frightened can find their own habits in the new arrangement. Legitimacy is manufactured before it is deserved, and a reformer who despises his audience will be removed by it.
observance: Elizabeth I inherited England after three religious settlements in twenty-five years and chose to give it a fourth that would hold for her whole reign. The Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity of 1559 broke with Rome and restored the Prayer Book of Edward VI, but she took the title Supreme Governor rather than Head, allowed wafer bread at communion, protected clerical vestments and church music, and left the traditional monuments standing in churches for a time. She stripped two bishops of their sees and summoned others before the Privy Council rather than sweeping the bench. The settlement satisfied neither the returned Protestant exiles nor the conservative Catholic nobility, and religious argument never entirely stopped. What it achieved was the absence of civil war, which France did not achieve over the same question, and which historians increasingly read less as a masterpiece of design than as a series of retreats forced by a parliament she could not yet control.
transgression: Thomas Cromwell served Henry VIII and, having spent a decade securing the succession and the divorce, was authorised to break with Rome and to dismantle the monasteries. He moved fast because the position demanded it, dissolving the smaller houses to finance the crown, producing a new nobility of Protestant gentry, and pushing an act of supremacy through a parliament that had never been asked to consider it. English parishes had watched the practice of the old religion for generations and had no intention of being told otherwise by a minister they had not chosen, and the gentry who had profited from the dissolutions were not yet secure enough to resist openly. By 1540 the conservative reaction had a focus: charges of heresy were laid before the king, and Cromwell was attainted and beheaded on Tower Hill. The reform had been real, and its speed produced the one man able to stop it.
reversal: Slow reform has a failure mode of its own, often worse than the abruptness the law warns against. A settlement designed to offend nobody offends nobody at any point, and a population never asked to make an effort never develops a stake in what it is doing. There is also a real cost in delay, and the argument about what people can bear is always available to those who benefit from the status quo. The distinction worth drawing is between pace and destination. Refusing to travel at all is not caution. The honest version of this law is to state the destination plainly, move as fast as consent allows, and accept that a settlement nobody can identify as new will be defended by nobody when the crisis comes.
keyTakeaways: Everyone endorses change in the abstract and resists it on a given Tuesday.
Keep the forms people recognise, and change what sits behind them.
A population told for years that it is being improved will resist on principle.
Name the destination plainly; a settlement nobody sees as new will be defended by nobody.

title: Never appear too perfect
summary: Envy is quiet, patient and near. Show an ordinary fault or two, or let the people beside you feel their chance has gone.
core: Almost any visible superiority creates resentment, and flawless superiority creates it in the group least likely to be suspected and best placed to do harm. The envious cannot acknowledge what he feels, since to admit envy is to admit inferiority, so it goes underground and appears as criticism, as praise too emphatic, as a convenient story about how you made your way, and eventually as quiet sabotage. The prescription is disarmament through imperfection. Display an ordinary defect, admit a harmless vice, attribute the important part of any success to luck or to other people, and let observers see a man with edges they recognise. A person others can measure is safer than one they cannot, because envy attaches to the unmeasurable.
observance: Cosimo de' Medici made it deliberate policy that nobody in Florence should be able to measure him. He was the richest man in Europe by any ordinary reckoning and he dressed soberly in local woollen cloth, avoided the ornament Florentine fashion permitted him, lived plainly, worked long hours and was accessible to the humblest citizens. Contemporary accounts describe him as unostentatious in public, while the portraits his bank financed present a far more imposing image, and the discrepancy was the point. His contemporaries saw a modest banker and a few sitters saw something else entirely. He gave large sums to churches and religious orders, which Florence read as piety and which converted a dangerous fortune into a civic reputation. He died in 1464 and the city decreed that Pater Patriae be inscribed on his tomb.
transgression: Joe Orton was thirty-four and at the height of his fame when his partner of sixteen years killed him with nine blows from a hammer in the flat they shared in Islington on 9 August 1967, then took an overdose of barbiturates. Orton had gone from the prison sentence they received together in 1962 for defacing library books to the most performed new playwright in the English language, and Halliwell, the older man who had been his mentor, watched the whole movement without arriving in it. Orton's plays were praised to the skies, his private diaries printed a life that had previously been closeted, and producers and actors entered a circle that had been two people. Whether the act was envy of the success or the sense of being left behind is still debated, since the final pages of the diary Halliwell referred to are missing. The discrepancy had been visible and unmanaged for years.
reversal: Manufactured modesty is the trap inside the trap. False humility reads as insecurity, which deepens the very feeling of superiority it was meant to relieve, and people who dislike the display also dislike being managed. The gesture must be a real concession, and there are those who cannot make one: a person whose achievements are genuinely rare cannot pretend to a fault without the pretence being obvious. The reverse error also needs naming, the habit of displaying faults nobody was going to suspect. The point is not to become small but to remain legible as a person, with limits others can find, so that the envy has somewhere honest to sit.
keyTakeaways: Flawless superiority breeds envy in the group best placed to act on it.
Envy goes underground and returns as criticism, rumour and quiet sabotage.
Show an ordinary fault, or attribute the important part of the success to luck.
A person others can measure is safer than one they find impossible to measure.

title: Do not go Past the Mark you Aimed for; In Victory, Learn when to Stop
summary: Victory is the moment of maximum risk, because the feeling of it distorts the judgement that earned it.
core: The point of maximum danger is the moment of success, not the moment of crisis. Momentum is mistaken for destiny and elation for proof, and a man who has been recently fortunate concludes that fortune will continue on request. He presses past the mark he set for himself, and each additional enemy is a new claim on a limited supply of energy, goodwill and time. The law is therefore a discipline of definition. Know before you begin what the objective is, recognise it when it is reached, and stop. The mark need not be a place on a map; it may be a concession obtained or a rival silenced. The rare quality is not the advance but the withdrawal, and a victory pursued too far produces a defeat that erases the victory which preceded it.
observance: Pericles conducted the naval campaigns of the 430s BC at a deliberate distance from the frontier of Athenian appetite, sailing into the Black Sea, subduing Sinope, protecting the grain route and returning, while the assembly in Athens began to dream of Egypt, Sicily and Carthage. He argued against expansion and accepted the odium of it, telling the Athenians they would win if they waited, kept to the navy and attempted no new conquests during the war. He also understood the need for the appearance of movement, winning small engagements that could be presented as continued success without committing the city to a campaign it could not hold. After his death in 429 the argument was lost. The successors adopted the demagogy he had avoided, overrode him, and sent the great armada to Syracuse, where it was destroyed in 413. The restraint was worth the empire it preserved.
transgression: Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid empire, had overthrown the Medes, the Lydians under Croesus and the Babylonians, and had established himself as the most successful ruler the world had seen. Around 530 BC he turned to the northeastern frontier and campaigned against the Massagetae, whose queen Tomyris refused his proposal of marriage and warned him to be content with his own kingdom. He crossed the river, and when Croesus advised a manoeuvre using wine against a people unacquainted with it, the camp was taken and Tomyris' son Spargapises was captured and killed himself. Herodotus has the queen swear by the sun that she will give him his fill of blood, gather her army and defeat him; and in the account he thought most credible the Persians were destroyed and Cyrus killed in the greatest battle he ever fought.
reversal: Restraint has a counterfeit, which is the excessive caution that arrives with a victory and freezes the victor. A man who stops at the mark once may reasonably stop twice, and the habit turns into timidity, the initiative passes to whoever is still prepared to move, and the defensive posture that followed the last success becomes the reason for the next failure. Nor is the mark always visible from inside the moment, which is why it must be written down beforehand rather than inferred from whatever appears to have happened. One situation overrides the rule. An enemy left alive and unanswerable returns, and partial punishment that produces a grievance without removing a danger is the worst of both. Crush or leave alone; the middle course manufactures a revenge.
keyTakeaways: Define the mark before you begin, and stop the moment it is reached.
Momentum gets mistaken for destiny, and each extra claim drains limited reserves.
The rare quality is the withdrawal rather than the advance.
Write the mark down beforehand, since it is hard to see from inside the moment.

title: Assume Formlessness
summary: Whatever takes a fixed shape can be studied, anticipated and struck. Stay fluid until you choose the moment to condense.
core: A plan with a visible shape is a plan an opponent can study. He can anticipate it, prepare against it and choose the moment to strike, and the more fixed your behaviour becomes the fewer options you retain. Formlessness is the deliberate refusal to hold a single shape: dispersal, mobility, an unpredictability that makes the other party reveal his own intention in the effort to find yours. Water is the model, since it yields to every obstacle without ceasing to be water. The judgement carries a warning, which is why the law comes last. None of the others is a form to be kept; they are postures appropriate to a moment, and a strategy practised until it becomes a habit has become the fixed shape this law exists to avoid.
observance: T. E. Lawrence did not command the Arab Revolt of 1916 to 1918 so much as decline to have a form to attack. He worked through Emir Faisal rather than issuing orders, because a British officer openly leading tribal irregulars would have turned a national rising into an imperial one and cost the revolt the sympathy it depended on. In councils he fed in an idea and let the Arabs argue it until it appeared to be their own. He adopted the smallest force in the quickest time at the farthest point, striking the Hejaz railway with charges designed to need hours of repair rather than moments, refusing to take Medina and content to have the line kept working at the maximum of loss and discomfort. The Turkish army had to hold a front running along parallel rails for fifty miles, then a hundred, then several hundred, and the irregulars moved like vapour along it.
transgression: Agesilaus II ruled Sparta for forty-one years and defended its post-war hegemony with a constancy that became the definition of the man. He campaigned in Asia, fought in the Corinthian War, used the clause of the Peace of Antalcidas guaranteeing the independence of the Greek cities to force the dissolution of the Boeotian League, and reduced Thebes to starvation in two sieges. When Thebes was conspicuously left out of the congress of 371 BC his refusal to let the Thebans sign for Boeotia precipitated the war in which Cleombrotus was destroyed at Leuctra by an army half the size of the Spartan force. He was given full powers to reform the constitution and Plutarch's verdict is that he lacked the imagination required. Sparta was freed of the Messenians in the following decade, destroying the labour its economy rested on, and he ended his days as a mercenary general.
reversal: Formlessness without a centre is merely aimlessness, and water with nothing to be contained by spreads out and disappears. A leader who changes position with every current keeps nothing and defends nothing, and the people who took his measure will stop distinguishing between his substance and his changes. The flexibility is external; the purpose behind it must remain fixed or the performance is a sham. A second cost is that others cannot read it: constant unpredictability deprives allies of any means of coordinating with you. The practical rule is to stay formless while you are weaker or more numerous, take a definite shape when you concentrate your force to strike, and disperse again at once.
keyTakeaways: Any plan with a visible shape can be studied, anticipated and struck in advance.
Refuse to hold one fixed posture, so the other side reveals his intention hunting yours.
A strategy practised until it is a habit has become the fixed shape to avoid.
Stay fluid while weaker, take shape to concentrate a strike, then disperse at once.
